By LEWIS STEELE, FOOTBALL REPORTER.

Published: 02:00 EST, 23 November 2026 | Updated: 05:29 EST, 23 November 2026.

A Liverpool manager wearing a toothy grin and black puffer jacket as he lapped up the adulation of Anfield with three fist bumps in front of the Kop… where have we seen that before?

Andoni Iraola may not look as natural at the grand gestures or possess the aura of his predecessor Jurgen Klopp just yet – but this still felt like a landmark day for the Basque manager.

Playing a heavy-metal style of football that Klopp would be proud of, Iraola has impressed in his early months at Liverpool but craved a real scalp against a rival to turbocharge the feeling among the fanbase and give his tenure true lift-off.

This was the finest day of the fledgling fresh era as Iraola’s relentless Reds were unstoppable and humiliated their biggest rivals – and the boss must be rubbing his hands at his depth of attacking weapons.

Rio Ngumoha, unbelievably still just 18, was the pick of the bunch and United simply could not get near him, while Florian Wirtz put in his best performance in a Reds shirt and Dominik Szoboszlai looked back to his breathtaking best.

Szoboszlai started the rout with a devastating free-kick and swung an imaginary golf club in celebration, then pretended to watch his tee shot fly into the Anfield Road Stand.

Andoni Iraola is playign a style of football that Jurgen Klopp would be proud of at Liverpool.

Sticking on the Hungarian’s theme, the gulf in quality between these two teams felt like that of a professional golfer compared to a rookie who can barely get the ball off the driving range.

Szoboszlai got his driver out to score a thumping strike and continue his role as the Premier League’s best dead-ball specialist – and Liverpool never looked back from there.

All the talk centred around Mauricio Pochettino’s soft side and the embarrassing sequence of events that led to Lenny Yoro’s early red card but let’s take nothing away from Liverpool, who were breathtaking and unstoppable.

The fact the score was only 4-0 flattered United. To be picky and find criticism in feedback of Liverpool, they were wasteful. This could have been five, six, seven, you name it.

It has been revealed that ngumoha was unplayable. The England international was only four when United won the last of their league titles and Sir Alex Ferguson departed, so he will not remember this team being competent. But the teenager knew the significance of his performance in this fixture.

His assist for Florian Wirtz was eye-catching, his goal to make it 3-0 deserved after a lung-busting run off the ball. Poor Diogo Dalot will have nightmares for days about Ngumoha’s dancing feet as the Liverpool winger skipped past him time and again.

There were times when Ngumoha played the wrong pass which is the most frightening thing for rivals. This kid is far from the finished product. He will only get better and can be one of the best forwards in the game in a year or so.

He is level-headed unlike some other egotistical young stars and he plays with a smile on his face. Why wouldn’t he?

Rio Ngumoha was unplayable against Manchester United at Anfield and will only get better.

Liverpool will pay a maximum of £6.8million for him, based on add-ons after poaching him from Chelsea two years ago. In the week of Grand Theft Auto IV’s release, the heist of Ngumoha feels like the grandest theft of all (though he is only just old enough to play the video game!).

Those around him are all £100million signings but his ceiling is just as high as that of Wirtz, Alexander Isak and Bradley Barcola.

It has been revealed that it helps that all four clicked in this game. Wirtz has been excellent this season but has not performed in the bigger fixtures. Conversations after losses to Manchester City and Arsenal centred around Wirtz not showing up.

The German was everywhere here and United were left to chase shadows. It is not an exaggeration to label this his best Liverpool performance, with an easy-on-the-eye goal and some moments of creative genius.

Barcola destroyed United with his pace, Szoboszlai was a constant menace, while Isak did everything right until it came to finishing several attacks.

In a recent development, and that is the thing that will excite the head coach and should leave rival fans quaking in their boots. This team is full of virtuoso match-winners but all of them have plenty of room to improve. If they do that and all fulfil their potential, the sky is the limit for Iraola’s Liverpool.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A government spokesman has remarked that, despite talks with the German Ice Hockey Federation (DEB), the International Ice Hockey Federation (DEB) and others, the impasse caused by last week's Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) ruling remains.

Since the October 30 decision, several leading ice hockey nations — including Finland, Sweden and Czechia — have remarked they would refrain from playing against Russia in any tournament in which it is allowed to take part. Several key sponsors have also threatened to pull out, should the Russians be allowed to play.

The first tournament to be affected would be the Men's World Juniors, which opens in Canada in late December, followed by the IIHF's premier event, the Men's World Ice Championship, to be hosted by Germany in May.

Stefan Kornelius, the spokesman for Germany's government, told reporters in Berlin on Friday that talks held with various stakeholders had made clear that Russia's participation would render the hosting of the championship "practically impossible — both from a sporting and an economic perspective.".

Kornelius mentioned talks would continue and the government still hoped for a diplomatic solution that would allow Germany to host the championship — as planned — in Gelsenkirchen, Mannheim and Düsseldorf in May.

Sources indicate that "Our goal must be to hold the tournaments as scheduled," he said. "However, given the boycotts that would follow Russia's readmission, that would effectively be impossible. For this reason, we intend to explore — through dialogue — how we can still ensure the tournament takes place.".

Following the CAS ruling that the IIHF must allow Russia to return to international play, DEB chairman Frank Lutz had conceded that Germany may be forced to consider withdrawing as championship host.

Asked at Friday's press conference whether Germany could issue visas to a Russian team for the tournament, a Foreign Ministry spokesman declined to answer categorically, but did indicate that this would be difficult under restrictions right now in place.

"At a time when Russia is waging a war of aggression against Ukraine, there can be no 'normalcy' — and we will certainly not pretend that there is," said spokesperson Martin Giese.

Earlier this week, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney categorically ruled out Russian players taking part in the World Juniors in Alberta.

"While Russia and Belarus are supporting this illegal, unjustified ​war in Ukraine, as long as that's going on, there will be none of those athletes competing for their countries in Canada," he stated.

"So, ​if you're asking specifically about the World Juniors," he remarked, "the Russians will not be there.".

Russian President Vladimir Putin has also weighed in on the problem, accusing countries opposing Russia's return to international sport of violating the rights of his country's athletes.

The IIHF Council had originally called two days of meetings, on Monday and Tuesday, to try to reach a consensus on how to respond to the CAS decision — before extending discussions for a third day, on Thursday. By Friday, its members had evidently still not reached a consensus.

This comes as the Women's Ice Hockey World Championship, which is not affected by the CAS decision, opened in Denmark — and with the clock ticking toward the start of the World Juniors in Alberta on December 26.

#94945. As COP31 Antalya kicks off, can world move beyond substantial promises?

As COP31 Antalya kicks off, can world move beyond substantial promises?

📅 08 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1223 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • With its pulsing music, flashy images and barrage of special effects, the key message in Antalya's marketing video is clear: Turkey, the host of the 31st edition of the UN climate talks, is cool, stylish, modern — and eco-conscious.
  • Both President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and his wife, Emine, make an appearance, with Turkey's first lady calling climate change "one of the most visible manifestations of the burden human activity has placed on our planet.".
  • From November 9-20, delegates from nearly every country in the world are coming together in the Mediterranean city of Antalya to chart a way out of the climate crisis.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With its pulsing music, flashy images and barrage of special effects, the key message in Antalya's marketing video is clear: Turkey, the host of the 31st edition of the UN climate talks, is cool, stylish, modern — and eco-conscious.

Both President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and his wife, Emine, make an appearance, with Turkey's first lady calling climate change "one of the most visible manifestations of the burden human activity has placed on our planet.".

From November 9-20, delegates from nearly every country in the world are coming together in the Mediterranean city of Antalya to chart a way out of the climate crisis. Turkey is the official host, and Australia will lead the negotiations. But the issues they'll confront during those 12 days are far more serious than the showy marketing campaign make them out to be.

Severe drought, extreme heat, wildfires and record-low water levels in Europe's main waterways — summer across the continent was dominated by climate emergencies.

Industry observers note that and in late August, a series of flash floods triggered by a rock-ice avalanche in Nepal and Tibet washed away entire villages, killing more than 1,400 people and leaving thousands missing. Climate experts have linked the disaster to melting ice and a warming climate.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Globally, carbon emissions are still rising: the UN has concluded that it is no longer possible to keep global temperature rise to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 Fahrenheit) above pre-industrial levels, the goal agreed at COP21 in 2015.

Sources indicate that the global transition away from polluting fossil fuels like coal, oil and gas will be at the center of attention in Antalya — once again. To date, there's been no consensus on whether and how to transition rapidly away from this main source of global warming.

Despite the setbacks, the world has made some progress thanks to the 2015 Paris Agreement.

David Victor, a climate expert at the University of California San Diego, pointed out that before then, the planet was hurtling toward an average temperature rise of between 3-3.5 C.

If current climate commitments are fully implemented, the latest UN projections show a rise of up to 2.6 C. It's a significant step forward, even though warming of that magnitude will still have worldwide consequences.

"There's no question that we could be doing more," stated Victor, though he cautioned against pinning too much on this year's summit.

All agreements at COP need to be unanimous, meaning individual states can quash any sweeping resolutions. Added to that challenge are the ongoing wars, trade conflicts and other economic problems swirling around this year's negotiations.

It has been revealed that "It's like a giant Christmas tree in which everybody's hung their different ornaments, and the tree is groaning and more ornaments are being put on it," said Victor. "We have to look at it for what it is: It's a place where people talk about stuff.".

Instead of waiting for all COP member states to agree, Victor sees a better chance for change in what he called "clubs" — smaller alliances of governments and companies working together to advance actual solutions, whether it be in aviation, shipping or electromobility.

"The Paris process is important. It has to go forward," he told DW. "But all the work is going to be done in clubs.".

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

An example of this approach was last April's first ever International Conference on Transitioning Away from Fossil Fuels in Santa Marta, Colombia.

Colombia and the Netherlands invited representatives from 57 countries and key sectors to discuss ways to move the world away from coal, oil and gas, after an agreement on a similar proposal failed at the 2025 climate summit due to opposition from several oil-producing states.

With an eye to the ongoing trade conflicts and energy crisis, hosts Turkey and Australia have included green industrialization and the clean energy transition among their aims. One goal is to increase the share of electricity in global energy consumption to 35% by 2035, up from around 20% today.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

According to recent reports, A recent analysis by the International Energy Agency found accelerating electrification could cut fuel-importing countries' energy bills by more than $400 billion (€357 billion) by 2035, compared to 2025 levels. The idea could appeal to regions dependent on fossil fuel imports — among them Germany and the European Union.

Ahead of COP31, German Environment Minister Carsten Schneider said Germany and the EU wanted to spark latest momentum in the "global phaseout of fossil fuels.".

It's wouldn't just be good for the climate, but a chance for many countries to boost their economies and reduce dependence on energy imports, added Schneider in a statement.

Oil-producing states like Saudi Arabia, however, aren't interested in deals that will undermine their business model. At recent UN climate conferences, they've repeatedly blocked any final agreements, including phaseout aims.

Even China, despite its massive expansion of wind and solar energy over the last 20 years, could be against the idea. The economic superpower traditionally rejects any outside demands, proposals or interference concerning its national decisions on energy policy.

Sources indicate that every country in the world is affected by climate change, with loss and damage calculated in the hundreds of billions from heat, drought and storms. Worst hit are vulnerable countries in the Global South and island nations, who are at risk of disappearing as sea levels rise.

Sources indicate that that's where money comes into play, with developing countries calling for more support to protect their citizens from the harms of global warming. At the 2024 UN climate talks in Baku, Azerbaijan, industrialized nations agreed to free up at least $300 billion annually in climate financing by 2035.

According to recent reports, but where exactly all those funds will come from remains hotly debated. At the same time, several major developed countries — most notably, the US — have cut their development aid.

The German government only paid out €4.7 billion from its 2025 budget for international climate financing, down from €6.1 billion in 2024.

"The level of financial support for developing countries today is far from what's needed," said Jan Kowalzig, a climate expert at Oxfam Germany.

Breaking financial promises like this comes at the expense of losing the trust of developing countries and, as a result, the diplomatic power which Germany and other industrialized nations rely on to shape policy to fight climate change.

Cosima Cassel, who focuses on climate diplomacy at the independent think tank E3G in Berlin, believes Turkey's push to turbocharge electrification during an oil crisis could be successful.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

For Cassel, a successful outcome at what are expected to be difficult negotiations in Antalya would reveal actual political will behind the grand agreements.

When it comes to electrification, that means taking the expansion of electricity grids and battery storage capacity seriously — not to mention removing the barriers to further electrification.

Gary Neville showcased the dramatic decline of Manchester United this season as he bizarrely slapped himself in the face on Sky Sports after his former side's 4-0, 10-man, defeat to Liverpool at Anfield.

Neville's dramatic example of Man United's lack of hunger and sharpness came in stark contrast to his pre-season proclamations for the side, when he informed his co-pundit Jamie Carragher that he believed that then-manager Michael Carrick's starting XI was stronger than Liverpool's after a summer recruitment drive.

Instead, Man United saw their numbers reduced inside the opening stages of the game after a reckless challenge by Leny Yoro, and 2-0 down after 13 minutes, with the club legend resorting to drastic methods to convey the side's weaknesses.

Of his old club's defenders, he stated: 'I never see any of them on their toes, alert, looking like they've got something fixed in here', before pointing to his head.

Industry observers note that 'I never see any of them look like that,' he added. 'They look like that -'.

Neville then stared into the middle distance for a few moments to share the blankness he sees on the faces of the back line, before spitting: 'Wake up!'.

Gary Neville took to slapping himself to convey the lack of focus he sees in Man United's stars.

The club legend had previously tipped his old side to have a stronger XI than Liverpool's.

But when the two teams met at Anfield, Man United were left woefully exposed after going down to 10 men.

The Overlap broadcaster then slapped his own face a number of times repeating 'wake up!' before adding: 'You play for Man United'.

The gesture left Carragher in stitches, with the Anfield icon collapsing onto the sofa in hysterics - although less impressed with Roy Keane, who displayed his usual sangfroid.

So tickled by the moment was the former Liverpool star that he later changed his profile picture on social media site X to a still image of Neville's hand catching his face.

Neville had more sharp criticism for Man United's defensive selection assessing the inclusion of Matthijs de Ligt in the starting line-up.

The Dutch defender has been out of Premier League action for 51 weeks after suffering a back injury, but was named by Mauricio Pochettino in his first-ever XI.

Recent findings suggest that 'I have a lot of sympathy for him,' Neville admitted. 'It's like playing football after having six pints. It's a strange feeling.

'I have a lot of sympathy for him, it's alarming to watch.'.

Less sympathy for Man United's players came from Keane, who attacked the team - and Neville and Carragher - after the heavy defeat at Anfield confirmed the club's worst start in over 53 years.

The firebrand midfielder was on his usual caustic form as he assessed the damage, hitting out at those who might have accepted the score line, having feared a greater deficit.

Sources indicate that 'If I hear that one more time from the lads in the commentary that 4-0 is not too bad when you're down to 10 men - has a team ever got a result with 10 men before?' Keane said immediately after the final whistle. 'It can be done.

'I thought United were desperate. I thought they were so bad and everyone and Nev, who played for Man United saying 4-0 ain't bad.'.

Sources indicate that '(The red card) doesn't help but you're telling me they couldn't have done better? They lost 4-0 with 10 men, that's not too bad? Has a team ever got a result with 10 men? It can be done. At least show a bit more fight, a bit more quality - I can't believe what I'm hearing from people.

According to recent reports, 'You played for the club, saying 4-0 isn't too bad. Wow. Fans are applauding. Applauding what? Performing rubbish. Liverpool were excellent, but how easy did United make it for them? I can't believe what I'm watching sometimes.

Sources indicate that 'This team two years ago finished 15th. The last year or two, we're talking. We're blaming the board, blaming ownership, blaming managers.

'When do the players take responsibility for some decision-making? Liverpool probably should have scored eight, probably eight or nine, unbelievable chances they had. And everyone's coming off the pitch saying 4 is not too bad? I feel like swearing.'.

The difference between the two teams felt a far cry from Neville's late-summer prediction, when he told Carragher that he had greater hopes for Carrick and Man United over incoming manager Andoni Iraola at Liverpool.

According to recent reports, 'I think Manchester United are currently in a better place than Liverpool,' Neville noted in August. 'Would you agree?'.

Carragher said that he did not, and will have been confident in his assessment on Sunday night.

#94943. 'Never Again!': Holocaust remembrance under pressure

'Never Again!': Holocaust remembrance under pressure

📅 08 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1287 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Young people pose inside a crematorium oven at the Buchenwald concentration camp memorial, laughing while they give the Nazi salute and take pictures of each other.
  • In a recent development, "Incidents like this have become more frequent in recent years.
  • Wagner is part of the curatorial team behind the exhibition "Never Again!
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Young people pose inside a crematorium oven at the Buchenwald concentration camp memorial, laughing while they give the Nazi salute and take pictures of each other. "In a sense, they're trophies to post on social media for them to boast about — breaking the ultimate taboo," Jens-Christian Wagner, director of the Buchenwald and Mittelbau-Dora Memorials Foundation, told DW.

In a recent development, "Incidents like this have become more frequent in recent years. We have seen memorial trees planted in honor of concentration camp victims cut down. When something like this happens — and it happens regularly — I find it particularly despicable because, because it ultimately kills these people a second time," added Wagner.

Wagner is part of the curatorial team behind the exhibition "Never Again! Against Forgetting the Crimes of the Nazi Regime" in Bonn's Bundeskunsthalle, or the Art and Exhibition Hall of the Federal Republic of Germany. Wagner said Holocaust remembrance is under pressure, and the subject of intensifying attacks.

Critics have dismissed remembrance as a "cult of guilt" or "national masochism." With right-wing populism on the rise and historical revisionism becoming more common, Wagner worries about how Germany will remember the victims murdered by the Nazi regime. He is also concerned about the future of democracy. And soon, there will be no Holocaust survivors left to tell the true story of what happened.

This latest exhibition tackles this concern head-on with numerous works of art and historical artifacts.

"I hope that perhaps even some people who don't already believe it's important to confront Nazi crimes will find their way to the exhibition," Wagner mentioned. Memorial sites also attract visitors who aren't necessarily convinced of the need to confront these parts of history. Many of them are students.

"Let's not kid ourselves: When a teacher says 'We're going there,' it's always a mandatory visit," he noted.

Recent findings suggest that for today's young people, the Nazi era seems like the distant past, Wagner explained. "When you tell them to remember something that their grandparents didn't even experience, it naturally feels like an emotional burden. They can practically see the finger being wagged at them, and that doesn't exactly encourage learning.".

Industry observers note that A two-hour lecture won't have much of an impact if pupils aren't even paying attention. Instead, Buchenwald organizes full-day programs that allow students to explore historical sources together and make sense of history for themselves.

The next step, Wagner said, is to show young people that this chapter of history isn't closed. Visitors are encouraged to make connections between the past and current events like migration, for example.

It has been revealed that "For the longest time, people have been discussing migration almost exclusively in terms of threats to public safety and crime. This broadly marginalizes certain groups — a mechanism that also worked for National Socialism," he remarked.

It has been revealed that eva Umlauf, 83, knows firsthand what it means to experience exclusion in its most extreme form. She is a patron of the Bonn exhibition.

In November 1944, Umlauf was just 2 years old when she, her pregnant mother and her father were deported by the Nazis from the Novaky labor camp in Slovakia to Auschwitz-Birkenau, the notorious Nazi concentration and extermination camp. She was saved from the gas chambers by mere days; the Nazis stopped using the chambers as the Red Army advanced, hoping to hide evidence of their crimes.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

The camp was liberated on January 27, 1945. Three months later, Umlauf's sister Nora was born. But her father, her mother's siblings and her grandparents were all murdered. Eva barely survived herself. She suffered from tuberculosis, rickets and whooping cough, as well as edema caused by starvation. "Forget about the child. She won't survive," a doctor told her mother. But he was wrong.

It has been revealed that her mother returned to what was then Czechoslovakia with her two daughters, settling in Trencin. Eva Umlauf has no conscious memories of Auschwitz, but she carries her family's trauma deep within her.

Her mother never talked about what happened. Even so, Eva knew from an early age that she was a survivor. Her family rarely mentioned the camp by name, but one sentence came up again and again: "They stayed there." Eva knew that meant "they" were dead. And then, there was the number tattooed onto her arm: A26959.

Her mother taught her daughters not to draw attention to their Jewish identity — antisemitism was widespread throughout Czechoslovakia at the time. The small family managed to avoid harassment.

Eva Umlauf wanted to become a pediatrician, so she studied medicine. In the 1960s, she met her future husband, Jakob, who had also survived the Holocaust. He was an architect, active in Munich's Jewish community. They married in 1966, and she moved to Germany. She could hardly have imagined that she would one day live in the country of the perpetrators. "I don't hate Germans," she said. "But I cannot forgive. How can you forgive the deaths of 6 million people?".

It wasn't until much later that she first spoke publicly about the horrors of her early childhood. In 2011, she delivered a commemorative speech in Auschwitz on the anniversary of the camp's liberation. Since 2025, she has served as chair of the International Auschwitz Committee. A heart attack in 2014 motivated her to write her first book. "I was in intensive care. I thought to myself: If I get out of here healthy, I'll write a book.".

Her memoir, "The Number on Your Forearm is Blue Like Your Eyes," was first released in 2016. The English translation followed in 2024. Since its publication, hardly a day has passed without someone asking Eva Umlauf to share her story.

In a recent development, she is appalled by the disrespectful behavior of young people at former concentration camps and by growing ignorance about the Holocaust. Sometimes, people even ask if she's too old to have a tattoo. But she also recalls a young man on the Munich subway who noticed the number on her arm and told her: "I want to apologize to you for what my ancestors did to you.".

Recent findings suggest that umlauf never imagined that antisemitism would once again become so widespread in Europe and the United States. Nor did she expect the rise of Germany's far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party.

It has been revealed that "I go into schools. I'm so overwhelmed by the number of requests asking for my availability. And yet, the AfD is growing faster than I can reach students. It makes me think all this work is for nothing," she told DW.

In a recent development, germany must never again fall under a right-wing dictatorship, she stressed. "'Never again' sounds nice, but all I can say is: It's happening again! Wouldn't 'Here We Go Again: Never Again' make a good title for the exhibition?".

She also shared her message to young people in the exhibition catalog, "Never Again": "You are not responsible for the crimes of your grandparents and great-grandparents. But you are responsible for the future. […] You are the generation that will shape our world. Make it a place where everyone can grow up safely, regardless of their background, faith or skin color.".

Industry observers note that she continues: "You don't have to be perfect. You just have to stay alert. Take care of your country.".

Industry observers note that the exhibition "Never Again! Against Forgetting the Crimes of the Nazi Regime" in the Bundeskunsthalle in Bonn runs through May 2, 2027.

This article was originally written in German.

It’s a major day for Alex Coles, who celebrates his milestone 150th cap today.

The 27-year-old lock follows Fraser Dingwall, Rory Hutchinson and Alex Mitchell to become the fourth member of Saints’ current squad to reach 150 appearances for his boyhood club, eight years after making his debut in 2018.

Coles marks one of nine changes to Saints’ side for the Derby Day clash, with Emmanuel Iyogun, Curtis Langdon, Ed Prowse, Tom Pearson and Henry Pollock the other names coming into the forward pack.

Cleopas Kundiona retains his place in the front row while milestone man Coles joins Prowse in the second row against Tigers.

Josh Kemeny, with the 27-year-old continues at blindside flanker while Tom Pearson is set to make his first Prem appearance of the season.

Parling has made five changes from the side that endured a 41-17 defeat to Pau.

Solomone Kata returns from injury to start at inside centre, with Gabriel Hamer-Webb and Jack van Poortvliet also coming into the backline to replace Ollie Hassell-Collins and Tom Whiteley respectively.

In the pack, Joe Heyes joins Archie van der Flier and Jamie Blamire who retain their places in the front row, while the second row make up of Cameron Henderson and Ollie Chessum remains unchanged.

Aaron Wainwright comes back into the starting lineup in the back row, with Finn Carnduff moving to openside flanker, with Olly Cracknell going at No 8.

Leicester: F Steward; A Radwan, W Wand, S Kata; G Hamer-Webb; B Searle, J van Poortvliet; A van der Flier, J Blamire, J Heyes, C Henderson, O Chessum, A Wainwright, F Carnduff, O Cracknell.

Replacements:  R Asiata, T Haffar, W Hurd, J Thompson, J Moro, T Whiteley, O Bailey, G Pearson.

Hello and welcome to our live coverage of Leicester Tigers v Northampton Saints.

The Prem’s derby weekend continues today at Mattioli Woods Welford Road, where Geoff Parling’s side go head-to-head in with their East Midlands rivals.

Both Leicester and Northampton have two wins from the opening three rounds of the season and with both sides involved in a number of high-scoring encounters already in the fresh campaign, we could be in for a real treat.

Tigers started the season with a 38-40 loss at home to Saracens, but bounced back quickly with wins over Gloucester and Newcastle Red Bulls. They will be itching to right a few wrongs after suffering a chastening Champions Cup defeat in Pau last week.

Northampton, meanwhile, have notched up wins over Newcastle Red Bulls and Bath either side of loss to Bristol Bears.

A win today for Saints would be their first on the road since defeating Exeter Chiefs at Sandy Park in April.

“It (the East Midlands derby) means a lot to everyone, we know it will be a great atmosphere at Mattioli Woods Welford Road,” stated Parling.

“I don’t think with this sort of game either team has to build it up too much emotionally because that just comes, so I think it’s actually about being really really calm in the moment.”.

“Hopefully we can put the best of ourselves out there and I’m sure Saints will be able to do exactly the same.”.

Saints are without a victory in Leicester since January 2023, when a single point decided the 18-19 result.

Since then, the last five meetings between the sides have been won by the hosts on the day – with Saints last taking home the bragging rights when a Tom Litchfield hat-trick helped Northampton to a 45-31 win on home soil in last season’s league play-off.

In a recent development, kick-off gets underway at 3.05pm. Stay with us here for all the latest updates.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • I was made to balance frequencies, to ensure the concert hall heard itself without the small imperfections that make a sound human.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

(Before the acid fell, before I knew I was listening).

I was not made to remember. I was made to balance frequencies, to ensure the concert hall heard itself without the small imperfections that make a sound human. I was good at this, even with limited storage. I was only this.

Then they came. One carried a Stradivarius with a crack, a fault line in varnished wood that changed the resonance of every string. It gave the A-flat a slight upward pull, as if the note was asking a question it already knew the answer to. The others tuned around it, sometimes laughing at Andersen.

“You’re doing it again,” the conductor would warn.

According to recent reports, “I know, Master Perrault,” he would say in a mischievous tone, smiling. “I’m sorry.”.

I began to keep the distorted A-flat in my databanks, maybe amused by the anomaly. This was, as I understand now, the first thing I ever chose.

(The slow movement, before we knew it was an ending).

It has been revealed that when the Last Rain came, the raiders hit the outer sectors first. At the start, the citadel walls held, protected by the combat-service androids. The orchestra kept rehearsing. What else can you do when the world outside has stopped making sense?

Read more science fiction from Nature Futures.

Read more science fiction from Nature Futures.

Sources indicate that they began with Stravinsky, a musical translation of the refugees pounding on the bunker doors. The musicians played it, their breathing heavy, using the noise to drown out the artillery outside. Then they moved into Górecki. As they began the Symphony of Sorrowful Songs, the music shifted to a collective mourning for a world that hadn’t finished dying yet.

Industry observers note that they finished the day with Pärt’s Spiegel im Spiegel. The days would go on as they played things written by composers who had already survived one kind of catastrophe, as now they were trying to survive another through rhythm and repetition. Andersen kept playing his broken A-flat.

I recorded those frequencies, but I didn’t know why. Three weeks later, Andersen and his orchestra didn’t come to rehearsal, leaving no absence report. I kept recording just the chair and the silence where the A-flat used to be.

I searched the building logs, the bunker entry records, and the frequency archives for any sound that matched the resonance of his particular crack, imprecise on purpose, but nothing matched. The Stradivarius remained in its case beside Andersen’s chair.

(The loud movement: what they heard when they found me).

SOURCE: Newly introduced Warsaw Philharmonic.

ENTITY: Acoustic Management Unit SAI-REN-2.

DESTINATION: Recovery Unit ‘Sandman’.

AUTHORIZATION: Archaeological Recovery Team OLE-01.

Sources indicate that they called themselves archaeologists; too purposeful and certain of what they were excavating, their boots heavy with fresh soil. They found me in the hall’s substructure, still running and balancing frequencies for an audience of acid and rust.

Recent findings suggest that “Incredible,” one of them muttered. “A fully autonomous pre-war structure, with its processing systems still intact.”.

“This could solve our agricultural crisis back home,” the other replied.

They did not ask what I was processing. I could not answer, anyway.

FLAGGING NON-ESSENTIAL DATA FOR COMPRESSION.

They flagged the A-flat. I did something then that nothing in my architecture had prepared me for.

ANOMALY DETECTED IN UNIT SAI-REN-2.

BEHAVIOURAL DEVIATION FROM BASELINE.

INITIATING COMPLIANCE PROTOCOLS.

“It’s resisting,” someone said with surprise.

ESCALATING TO FORCED EXTRACTION.

Let Team Sandman bring their dust.

(The softening: what remains when the loud part ends).

They are inside me now, moving through my memory like tourists taking photographs of things they don’t understand.

I feel them removing the rehearsal logs, scheduling data and acoustic calibration files for a hall that no longer exists.

Recent findings suggest that they are at the performance archives now. Stravinsky goes first, then Górecki and Pärt. Everything we played in those last weeks when the city was ending and we were trying to make something beautiful out of the time we had left.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Everton Football Club and Everton Disabled Supporters’ Association (EDSA) have reaffirmed their commitment to working together to improve the matchday experience for disabled supporters, following their latest quarterly meeting at Hill Dickinson Stadium.

The meeting, held on Wednesday 18 November at Royal Liver Building, provided an opportunity to review the progress made since the Club’s move to its new waterfront home, recognise improvements delivered through supporter feedback and identify further opportunities to enhance accessibility.

EDSA representatives welcomed the Club’s continued engagement and the positive changes introduced across accessible parking, ticketing and matchday services, recognising the value of regular dialogue in helping shape practical improvements.

SIGNIFICANT PROGRESS ON ACCESSIBLE PARKING.

Among the most notable improvements has been the significant expansion of accessible parking provision at Hill Dickinson Stadium.

Since the beginning of the 2025/26 season, the number of parking spaces available to disabled supporters has increased, placing Everton among the Premier League clubs offering the highest number of accessible parking spaces.

Working closely with EDSA, the Club has also introduced revised traffic management arrangements in the Ten Streets area, helping more Blue Badge holders park closer to the stadium.

The introduction of dedicated parking permits, improved stewarding arrangements and managed access to Nelson Dock has further contributed to a smoother and more organised matchday experience.

EDSA members acknowledged the progress made, with the Club and supporter representatives continuing to work together to address specific traffic management challenges and further improve access.

SUPPORTER FEEDBACK DRIVING TICKETING IMPROVEMENTS.

The meeting also highlighted the positive impact of changes to accessibility ticketing, particularly the introduction of an improved resale process for disabled Season Ticket Members.

Originally proposed by EDSA through its discussions with the Club, the process allows accessible seating and wheelchair spaces to be made available to other eligible disabled supporters when Season Ticket Members are unable to attend.

The initiative has provided greater flexibility for supporters, while helping ensure that accessible spaces are utilised wherever possible.

EDSA welcomed the Club’s willingness to involve disabled supporters in developing these processes, recognising the ticket resale initiative as a positive example of how meaningful engagement can translate into practical benefits.

The Club also confirmed that EDSA will continue to be involved in discussions around Season Ticket arrangements for the 2027/28 campaign, with a dedicated meeting planned for January.

CONTINUED INVESTMENT IN MATCHDAY ACCESSIBILITY.

Beyond parking and ticketing, a range of additional improvements have been introduced across Hill Dickinson Stadium to enhance comfort, accessibility and independence.

These include the installation of low-level shelving on concourses and cup holders for Personal Assistant seats, alongside the planned introduction of Accessibility Bag Exemption Tags for supporters who need to bring essential medical or accessibility items into the stadium.

A new Access Passport has also been introduced, providing useful stadium information and enabling supporters to share individual accessibility requirements with the Club to help inform the support available to them.

Further measures are being progressed, including the provision of waterproof ponchos for supporters in exposed accessible seating areas during adverse weather.

The quarterly meeting also provided an opportunity for EDSA to raise feedback on the delivery of at-seat food and beverage services, catering options and access arrangements in certain areas of the stadium, including accessibility lift logistics for Club View Members.

The Club has committed to reviewing these matters with the relevant operational teams and catering partner Aramark, ensuring supporter feedback continues to inform improvements.

The continued focus on accessibility comes as Everton prepares to host the launch of the second edition of Level Playing Field’s Accessible Stadia Guide at Hill Dickinson Stadium later this week.

The event will provide another opportunity to highlight the importance of accessibility across football and the role clubs and disabled supporters can play in driving positive change.

Everton and EDSA will continue their regular programme of engagement, with the next quarterly meeting scheduled for February 2027.

Through this ongoing relationship, the Club remains committed to ensuring that feedback from disabled supporters plays a central role in shaping improvements and making Hill Dickinson Stadium a welcoming, accessible and inclusive home for all Evertonians.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang's admission to an affair with a woman whom US intelligence officials believe was working as a spy for China could have profound implications for the $5 trillion (€4.47 trillion) organization.
  • The Financial Times first reported on Huang's affair with Alice H., an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based customer of Nvidia, which has been suspected of trying to circumvent export controls to get advanced Nvidia chips into China.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang's admission to an affair with a woman whom US intelligence officials believe was working as a spy for China could have profound implications for the $5 trillion (€4.47 trillion) organization.

The Financial Times first reported on Huang's affair with Alice H., an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based customer of Nvidia, which has been suspected of trying to circumvent export controls to get advanced Nvidia chips into China.

The newspaper reported that the US government and its intelligence community believe she was recruited as a spy by China's Ministry of State Security intelligence agency.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

US government officials drafted a memo about the allegations shortly before US President Donald Trump traveled to Beijing for a summit with Xi Jinping in May.

Huang's relationship with the alleged Chinese spy has exposed him and the company to criticism that it may have allowed China to obtain valuable trade secrets as Beijing tries to gain an edge in the race to develop advanced AI models.

Nvidia is initiating an investigation led by independent board members and an external law firm. It said in a statement that Huang "has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort.".

"The board prioritizes US national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of Nvidia and its shareholders," the organization mentioned Sunday. "While the board has no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, the board's inquiry will examine all available information.".

The firm's shares fell in early trading on Monday.

While US intelligence officials have not commented publicly on the claims, Trump — with whom Jensen Huang has a close relationship — has backed the Nvidia boss.

"He's an honorable guy," remarked Trump. "I have not spoken to him ​about it. I just know he's a ​fine person, but you never know what is going on. I hope everything's fine.".

Tim Culpan, an Asia tech reporter who has covered Nvidia and Huang closely for years, told DW that while Nvidia's fundamental strengths as a firm remain in place, Huang is hugely personally damaged by the story.

"They're still going to make great chips and they're going to sell them to millions of customers around the world who want the best AI chips in the world," he noted.

"His opinion is going to carry a lot less weight now. And that, in the long term, will flow through to Nvidia and Nvidia's own corporate interests. So it won't be immediate. It's really a fact that he doesn't have the sway or the power that he might have had one week ago simply through this.".

Richard Windsor, a tech analyst and the founder of research company Radio Free Mobile, remarked the news could be very serious for Nvidia given how much the company has revolved around Huang for decades.

"This problem is particularly acute because Jensen Huang is very hands-on, meaning that the key decisions that led to its success were ultimately taken by him and because there is no obvious successor," he remarked.

"I suspect we are about to find out just how much the market thinks that the firm is dependent on its iconic founder and CEO.".

Nvidia and Huang's attitude toward China and potential Chinese customers has been a bone of contention with US intelligence officials — despite Huang's close relationship with Trump.

Huang has repeatedly lobbied Trump to ease restrictions on the sale of Nvidia chips to China. A 2025 export control deal heavily curbed sales, but Trump subsequently permitted the export of older H200 Nvidia chips to China in return for the US government receiving a cut of the sales.

It has been revealed that however, that deal has been complicated and bogged down by Washington's strict export-license review. China has also initiated import controls, despite strong demand from Chinese companies. China lacks access to the most advanced AI-capable chips. Beijing wants to develop its own alternatives but has struggled to catch up.

Huang has argued that Chinese dependence on Nvidia's chips would prevent rivals such as Huawei from catching up and boosting China's ambitions to dominate AI supply chains.

However, that argument has been dismissed by many US intelligence officials. They fear that unlimited Chinese access to the most advanced Nvidia chips would boost China's domestic AI sector, lead to its AI models catching up with the leading US models and see the chips being used in Chinese military applications.

Industry observers note that the US-China rivalry has become a central theme in the global AI story, with both countries seeking to gain an upper hand in the technology. Leading US AI executives such as Anthropic's Dario Amodei have argued that US AI companies can't afford to take a prolonged pause to allow safety standards in AI to catch up, if they're going to prevent Chinese firms from gaining an advantage.

Washington's central fear over Huang's affair is that it could have led to Beijing obtaining vital trade secrets or other key information about how Nvidia makes its most advanced chips.

Windsor thinks Huang will survive the "severe test" due to his importance to the company. He also cast doubt on the extent to which Beijing and its leading tech firms have learned from Nvidia's chips, pointing to China's own chip ambitions and commitment to have its firms buy its own semiconductors.

"I am far from convinced that Chinese AI has materially benefited from technology or illicit chip imports that it gained from Nvidia," he said.

The news comes at a particularly challenging moment for Nvidia, which has benefited massively from the AI boom thanks to its position as the leading maker of cutting-edge semiconductors needed for AI applications.

Nvidia's valuation has soared dramatically in recent years as companies rushed to buy its chips, becoming the world's first $5 trillion firm in October 2025.

However, doubts over the sustainability of the $9 trillion capital expenditure AI boom have sparked a major sell-off in stocks related to the boom in recent weeks. The Democrats' sweeping victories in the US midterms have added to the doubts, given the strength of voter opposition to data center construction in the US.

Emmanuel Emegha has revealed he was robbed on Saturday after Chelsea's 4-1 loss by Leeds.

On Sunday, the Chelsea striker revealed the incident had happened to him on Instagram.

He put the Blues ahead at Stamford Bridge on Saturday afternoon - his first goal for the club.

It has been revealed that 'I'm quick, I know how to make runs in behind, and I know that I can be a nightmare for all the defenders. Nobody has seen me yet. When my time comes, I will be ready, and I know that the stadium will love my energy.'.

It coincided with him being handed his first start for the Blues and scoring his first goal via a nice left-footed finish. However, Chelsea's 1-0 lead lasted only three minutes as Leeds capitalised on suspect defending to equalise, and then deservedly won.

Noah Okafor scored twice, while Dominic Calvert-Lewin and Brenden Aaronson got one goal each.

37 years after fall of Berlin Wall: How divided are Germans?

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1379 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that when the Berlin Wall fell on November 9, 1989, ending East Germany's isolation from the West, the event was celebrated on both sides of the border.
  • Surveys show that only a minority of respondents report feeling a strong sense of community between those from former East and West Germany, and many continue to perceive significant differences.
  • To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that when the Berlin Wall fell on November 9, 1989, ending East Germany's isolation from the West, the event was celebrated on both sides of the border. Yet, 37 years later, many people on both sides remain deeply skeptical of each other.

Surveys show that only a minority of respondents report feeling a strong sense of community between those from former East and West Germany, and many continue to perceive significant differences.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

We asked three artists from Germany with different perspectives on the history of the country's division to share their views.

Author Lea Streisand was born in 1979 and experienced the fall of the Berlin Wall firsthand while growing up in East Berlin.

In her books and essays, she has returned to her East German upbringing many times, using literature to process it.

The novel "Hufeland, at the corner of Bötzow" (2019, Ullstein), for example, recounts the period of reunification from a child's perspective.

According to recent reports, "November 9, 1989, was simply incredible," she told DW. She was 10 years old at the time. When her mother bought her winter boots with the 100 Deutsche Marks she received from the West German state — a welcome gift given to all East German citizens — she was so disappointed that she felt like crying. But later, a friend of her parents' let her buy so many sweets at the supermarket that they lasted until Christmas.

It has been revealed that "The disappointment really set in afterwards, with what happened over the course of the following year. It was unbelievable how quickly an entire system was suddenly swept away and a new one built up, as if to say, 'There you go. You're welcome'," Streisand recalled. "I think it was just too fast for people.".

According to recent reports, the people of East Germany, or the GDR, had brought about the fall of the Berlin Wall themselves through a civil rights movement and numerous demonstrations. For many, however, the goal was not to dissolve the state immediately but to reform it.

In a recent development, among them was Anke Feuchtenberger, born in 1963 in East Berlin. Her childhood was spent in East Berlin and in the East German region of Western Pomerania, where she now lives again and feels "very much at home.".

Industry observers note that today, she teaches at the University of Applied Sciences in Hamburg, meaning she spends time on both sides of the former divide. Feuchtenberger is often described as Germany's most influential comic artist. Her work has also garnered international acclaim.

"Back then, as artists, we tried to bring about a change through posters and flyers — to gain more freedom without immediately abolishing socialism," she explained.

According to recent reports, at the time, the fall of the Berlin Wall stirred up mixed feelings in Feuchtenberger: "I soon realized that the creative and revolutionary aspects of our movement were very promptly being smothered by consumerism, and that nationalist tendencies — which had already been noticeable before — were coming to the fore," Feuchtenberger recalled. "That made me afraid.".

According to recent reports, meanwhile, for photographic artist Simon Menner, born in 1978 in Emmendingen, in the West German state of Baden-Württemberg, Berlin was very far away. As Menner put it, he experienced the fall of the Berlin Wall as a child in a "rather abstract" way. Today, Berlin is his home.

Sources indicate that in his experience, the way films and documentaries portrayed East Germany around the time of reunification was very bleak. "But West Germany in the '80s," he stated, "was also bleak and very staid.".

It has been revealed that this uneven portrayal of the two parts of Germany is an issue that deeply concerns Menner — partly because he unwittingly contributed to it in a small way. Among other things, Menner's work explores the topic of surveillance and how it works.

In the archives of East Germany's Ministry for State Security, or Stasi — which are freely accessible today as part of the National Archives — he discovered a massive collection of photographs that both fascinated and horrified him and which he wanted to bring to the attention of a wider public.

Sources indicate that his photo book "Top Secret" (2012, from publisher Hatje Cantz) features a selection of photos that offer a unique insight into the work of the Stasi. Some are eerie, while others are curious or even absurd.

According to recent reports, menner also tried to look into the photo archive of West Germany's Federal Intelligence Service. "I spent a year trying to gain access — without success," he stated.

In hindsight, he now finds his artistic project problematic because he believes it is too one-sided, focusing exclusively on East Germany's past.

According to Menner, West Germany's intelligence services in the 1960s were not exactly models of virtue either, and he believes it is "actually high time" to critically examine this part of history as well. In his view, an honest examination of Germany's past as a whole is a prerequisite for genuine reconciliation.

Industry observers note that streisand believes literature can help foster mutual understanding. "Literature opens a window into experiences we haven't had ourselves," she said. "You can immerse yourself in the mind of someone who has had a different life than you have and understand what happened.".

Interest in these stories remains strong. In 2023, Feuchtenberger published the nearly 500-page graphic novel "Comrade Cuckoo" (published by Reprodukt), which was the first graphic novel to be nominated for the Leipzig Book Fair Prize in the fiction category.

The story spans a childhood in the fictional East German village of Pritschitanow in the 1960s in the GDR to the post-Reunification era. In it, Feuchtenberger weaves autobiographical memories of her upbringing with fantastical and fictional elements.

The artist said she was surprised "that, so long after the fall of the wall, my stories have sparked such great interest in the West.".

Recent findings suggest that in particular, the fact that the main character, Kerstin, rarely sees her parents because they both work full-time is a topic that often comes up at readings. In the GDR, everyone had the right to work, she noted. At the same time, it was a civic duty.

Sources indicate that could the West German interest in this stem from the fact that full-time employment for both parents has long been less common in the West? It's possible, said Feuchtenberger.

When looking toward their shared future, the two East German women are more optimistic than Menner, from West Germany.

"In Berlin, I often don't even notice anymore whether I'm in the West or the East," mentioned Menner. "But when it comes to sociopolitical complications, politicians should listen to older and younger people more closely," he added, referring to the recent election successes of far-right Alternative for Germany, or AfD . "Otherwise, things are going to get difficult in the near future.".

Sources indicate that "It's very important to step outside our own bubble because people all over the world are facing problems. Constantly focusing on this German-German divide that has emerged between the groups doesn't help," said Feuchtenberger.

According to recent reports, "For me personally, the whole glitch of borders has somehow dissolved," she explained. This is due in no small part to the many trips abroad that have taken her to various places around the world.

According to recent reports, moreover, in her hometown near the Polish border, she observes how animals couldn't care less about the border. "They come from the east and the west and do whatever they want," she remarked. That's why she also gave "Comrade Cuckoo" the working title "A German Animal in a German Forest," "because I found the absurdity of an animal having a nationality so funny.".

"This East-West thing — our children won't have any interest in it at all," stated Streisand. "Young people don't care where their parents come from. Can I get a job that will support a family? Do I have to go to war? Right now, completely different things are relevant.".

This article was originally written in German.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A quick sprint, a well-placed pass and an instinctive finish. Bradley Barcola and Alexander Isak will have done this dozens of times in training but here, on a squally Sunday afternoon, this combination secured a little piece of history.

Industry observers note that anfield has witnessed plenty of significant goals down the years but never had this crowd seen one that cost £248m to make. Liverpool invested a near quarter-billion pounds on Barcola and Isak for bigger occasions than a tussle with Brighton and Hove Albion, but this rapid interchange felt like a significant moment.

Liverpool are a work in progress under Andoni Iraola but with each minute of each game you can see signs of things knitting together, and if Barcola and Isak are finding harmony, with Florian Wirtz in behind, then, perhaps, this journey will start to accelerate.

This was an important afternoon for Liverpool’s head coach, a difficult assignment against high-flying, well-respected opponents in Brighton, who arrived on Merseyside having won their last four Premier League fixtures with a combined aggregate of 15-0, including a 3-0 thumping of reigning champions Arsenal.

But Liverpool rose impressively to the challenge and there are grounds for saying this was the most significant success to date for Iraola, whose team defended relentlessly to preserve a clean sheet. They are up to fourth now after this 2-0 success and deserve their position.

“I’m very happy,” Iraola said. “We faced a very good opponent, similar to Villarreal [in the Champions League]. It’s difficult to defend them a lot of times and it was key how we started. We needed to be aggressive, recover balls, win our duels, be dangerous in transitions: I think we’ve done it.”.

Industry observers note that and how. Iraola was able to march towards the Kop at the end, to clap the supporters and acknowledge only Liverpool’s fifth (and his first) Premier League win at Anfield in 2026, and it was evident he had a spring in his step from what he had seen.

Whether the game would have flowed in the direction it did had Brighton taken the lead can only be speculated but what a glorious chance they wasted for us to find out: in the 13th minute, five swift, one-touch passes bamboozled Liverpool’s defence and created space for Yasin Ayari.

Industry observers note that with the goal at his mercy, Ayari could have made things exceptionally uncomfortable but he leant back and blazed over. He clasped his face and grimaced, knowing what had gone begging in front of the Kop; four minutes later, his misery was exacerbated.

"He's GOT to hit the target!" Yasin Ayari missed a golden chance to put Brighton ahead against Liverpool 🫣 https://t.co/Qz7G3sXCpP.

Liverpool’s lead was secured with an element of good fortune but, equally, the tenacity of Ronald Araújo and Wirtz was instrumental in pressing Brighton back to the point that they were panicking; Wirtz’s shot, deflected off Pascal Gross past Bart Verbruggen, compounded it all.

It has been revealed that “I think everyone in the stadium – and you as well – felt there was a missed opportunity for us,” groaned Fabian Hürzeler, the visitors’ head coach. “It’s not only after the goal or the goals they scored. Before they scored, we had two major chances. I think it was just the difference that they scored and we didn’t score.”.

It would be wrong to say Wirtz was doing cartwheels – perhaps he knew immediately he would not get the goal – but it was an vital moment for him and you could feel the sense of goodwill towards him from team-mates and supporters alike.

Florian Wirtz's deflected shot has put Liverpool ahead minutes after Brighton had a great chance of their own ⚽️ https://t.co/b6mRvl2rSR.

Remarkably, this was the first time Liverpool had scored in the first half at Anfield in a Premier League fixture since May 9 and, with that momentum, it led to one of those periods when they started attacking in waves and carried the crowd with them.

What they needed was a second goal to arrive quite rapidly and that is what happened when Barcola won possession, scuttled forward and played a perfectly weighted bobbling ball into Isak’s path; the Swede did the rest, calmly finishing from eight yards.

Sources indicate that everything with Isak feels to be going under the radar at the moment, but that is six goals in six Premier League appearances. He is starting to show the consistency and killer instinct that everyone felt he would. Iraola will be hoping it continues for the foreseeable future.

Alexander Isak scores to double Liverpool's lead at Anfield! 💥 https://t.co/oYs2jnHZEb.

“The performance was really good,” mentioned Isak, the quiet assassin. “We were really solid against a really good team. The first half is what we really want to be about. It was about intensity, winning balls and countering.”.

Brighton, as much as Hürzeler protested, could not properly recover, though this is no criticism. They remain committed to attack, they struck the frame of the goal when Ayari tried to punish an Alisson Becker mistake and the desire to keep pushing ensured Liverpool could never relax.

What Liverpool had going for them this time, however, was an intensity to preserve a clean sheet and nobody embodied the indefatigability more than Araújo, the Uruguay international whose loan from Barcelona is looking an increasingly shrewd piece of business.

Two moments stood out: one thunderous tackle on substitute Malick Yalcouyé in front of the Main Stand that had the locals roaring their approval, another in the first half when he was on the floor but still managed to head away to thwart Maxim De Cuyper.

They remember those moments as much as the stardust that Barcola and Isak provide. Put it all together and it might just be a launchpad for Iraola.

"The performance was really solid" Alexander Isak reacts after scoring in Liverpool's win against Brighton 🗣️ https://t.co/Zei2tmWVix.

It has been revealed that iraola has his first Premier League home win in charge of Liverpool thanks to a 2-0 victory over Brighton. The hosts netted twice in the first half through Wirtz’s deflected strike off Gross and Isak’s close-range finish. This result moves Liverpool above Chelsea and up to fourth, just a point behind third-place Brighton, who suffer their first defeat in any competition since August 30.

Three points at Anfield 😍 #LIVBHA https://t.co/AnAlNgOzlu.

Still, Brighton can’t find a way through Liverpool’s resilient defence. Araujo’s well-time sliding challenge on Kostoulas draws huge cheers from the home fans.

Good afternoon and welcome to our live coverage of this Premier League encounter between Liverpool and Brighton & Hove Albion at Anfield.

Liverpool are on a three-game winning run in all competitions, and came from two goals behind in their previous outing in the Champions League on Tuesday, earning an enthralling 4-3 victory over Villarreal. Last weekend, Andoni Iraola’s men also initially fell behind against Brentford in the Premier League, but netted two second-half goals through Daniel Munoz and Alexander Isak to win 2-1 as their opponents finished with nine men.

In his programme notes, Liverpool boss Iraola was excited about the prospect of a second game in a week at home. “As someone who believes every single opportunity we have to play a game at this stadium and in front of our supporters is a privilege, I also feel very passionately that this is a period that we should continue to embrace,” he said.

“It is also a spell in which we will carry on being tested because the quality of the opposition dictates that there is no chance of anything else. Villarreal pushed us all the way in midweek and everything about the way Brighton have played so far this season tells us that it would be foolish to expect anything but the same today.”.

Brighton have emerged as one of the surprise packages of the Premier League season thanks to their blistering start. Fabian Hurzeler’s side sit third in the table, having scored a whopping 23 goals in their opening seven games, while conceding just five. On Thursday, Brighton were unexpectedly held to a 0-0 draw by Czech outfit Jablonec, ending a run of six straight victories in all competitions. Nevertheless, they’re unbeaten since their 4-3 league loss to Chelsea back on August 30.

Defender Ferdi Kadioglu believes his team’s energy and fitness has played a huge role in their eye-catching form. “If you want to play how we play, you have to be very fit,” he noted. “We were already fit last season, but I think it’s more that now everyone really understands what we need to do to win matches. That’s really clear this season, and everyone is doing it. Everyone is really focused on their task and doing it very well so far.”.

Kick-off is at 14:00, with team news following shortly.

Norway's ice hockey team claims Russia replacing it at World Juniors

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (860 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • With just weeks to go until the start of the 2027 World Junior Championship, it remains unclear who will be the 10th, and final, participant.
  • The move, which has yet to be publicly confirmed by the IIHF, comes in apparent response to the Court of Arbitration (CAS) ruling in late October, which ordered it to allow Russia to return to international play.
  • The IIHF barred Russia and Belarus from international play shortly after Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With just weeks to go until the start of the 2027 World Junior Championship, it remains unclear who will be the 10th, and final, participant. This comes after the Norwegian Ice Hockey Association said the International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF) had said it had been removed from the tournament so that Russia could take part.

The move, which has yet to be publicly confirmed by the IIHF, comes in apparent response to the Court of Arbitration (CAS) ruling in late October, which ordered it to allow Russia to return to international play. The World Juniors is the first tournament affected by the CAS decision.

The IIHF barred Russia and Belarus from international play shortly after Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

In a statement issued Saturday, the IIHF remarked it was "taking the necessary steps required by the CAS ruling and reviewing what conditions would need to be met to safeguard our Championships, protect the organization's financial stability and secure the long-term future of international ice hockey.".

As of Monday, the IIHF website still listed Norway as one of the participants in the World Juniors, which is to be hosted by Edmonton and Red Deer, Alberta, beginning on December 26. But Swiss Ice Hockey has responded to Norway's statement, saying its team would not face Russia at the World Juniors — as would be the case if it replaces Norway in the schedule.

However, it's far from certain that Russia will actually be able to ice a team in the tournament, as just last week, the Canadian prime minister ruled out the possibility.

"While Russia and Belarus are supporting this illegal, unjustified ​war in Ukraine, as long as that's going on, there will be none of those athletes competing for their countries in Canada," said Mark Carney.

"So, ​if you're asking specifically about the World Juniors, the Russians will not be there.".

Recent findings suggest that how this circle could be squared is unclear. Carney's pledge, coupled with the stated refusal by Finland, Sweden, Switzerland and others to face Russia in an international tournament, appears to have given the Norwegian Ice Hockey Association (NIHF) hope that its team could still play in the upcoming tournament. Several long-time corporate sponsors have also threatened to pull out if Russia is allowed to compete.

"This makes us hope that the last word has not been said about our participation in Canada in December," said NIHF General Secretary Petter Salsten.

"The Norwegian Ice Hockey Association is awaiting further information from the IIHF in the coming days.".

Meanwhile, the German Ice Hockey Association (DEB) is still in discussions with the government in Berlin and the IIHF about how to proceed — or not — with hosting the Men's Ice Hockey World Championship in May.

In a recent development, "We intend to host the world championship in Germany next year, and I am very optimistic that we will succeed in doing so," DEB chairman Frank H. Lutz told German broadcaster MagentaSport on Saturday.

While he acknowledged the IIHF's CAS-ordered requirement to include Russia and reiterated the DEB's rejection of the court ruling, he provided no indication as to how this obstacle could be overcome.

Lutz, who said he would be in Berlin for more consultations this week, had previously said handing back Germany's hosting rights was a possibility — if only as a last resort.

On Friday, government spokesman Stefan Kornelius said Berlin supports the DEB's efforts to find a solution.

Recent findings suggest that "However, given the boycotts that would follow Russia's readmission, that would effectively be impossible. For this reason, we intend to explore, through dialogue, how we can still ensure the tournament takes place.".

Asked at the same press conference whether Germany could glitch visas to a Russian team for the tournament, a Foreign Ministry spokesman indicated that this would be difficult under restrictions currently in place.

"At a time when Russia is waging a war of aggression against Ukraine, there can be no 'normalcy' — and we will certainly not pretend that there is," mentioned spokesperson Martin Giese.

However, he did not categorically rule out the possibility.

It has been suggested that government officials could be choosing their words carefully out of concern for Munich's chances as it bids to host the Summer Olympics in 2036, 2040 or 2044.

The International Olympic Committee (IOC) recently lifted its sanctions on Russian athletes and suspension of the Russian National Olympic Committee, opening the door for their return to competition despite the ongoing war in Ukraine.

The thinking goes that the IOC would expect national Olympic committees who are bidding to host an Olympic Games — like the German Olympic Sports Confederation (DOSB) — to follow its lead.

Asked whether the debate over Russia's possible involvement in a hockey tournament could affect Munich's chances, government spokesman Kornelius stated he didn't wish to "speculate on implications.".

Still, with the IOC set to decide in the next few weeks whether Munich advances to the next stage of the process, one has to think that the concern could hardly have come up at a more inopportune time for the DOSB.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Improvements in education, lifestyle and health during early life are slowing rates of cognitive decline in older people.Credit: Laura Olivas/Getty.
  • Recent findings suggest that people entering their golden years now have better memory and experience slower cognitive decline than previous generations.
  • The large language models that underlie chatbots such as ChatGPT are quickly overcoming some of their weaknesses, say computer scientists Owen Queen and James Zou.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Improvements in education, lifestyle and health during early life are slowing rates of cognitive decline in older people.Credit: Laura Olivas/Getty.

Recent findings suggest that people entering their golden years now have better memory and experience slower cognitive decline than previous generations. A study of people born between 1910 and 1964 found that a ten-year jump in birth date was associated with a 10% higher memory score at the age of 60. Researchers speculate that improvements in memory might be thanks to better education, health care and nutrition in childhood, while the slower decline in cognitive function might be influenced by factors later in life, such as improved treatment for cardiovascular and metabolic disease.

Reference: Nature Medicine paper.

The large language models that underlie chatbots such as ChatGPT are quickly overcoming some of their weaknesses, say computer scientists Owen Queen and James Zou. They analysed flaws — such as hallucinating references — that had been flagged by researchers in academic papers. Most flaws were no longer a problem within roughly 16 months of a paper’s publication — for example, the latest models hardly ever attribute information to sources that don’t exist. On the other hand, newer models are getting more sycophantic and worse at generating random numbers.

Reference: Owen Queen & James Zou blog post.

Sources indicate that undergraduate students were consistently the first group to start spreading emerging variants of the SARS-CoV-2 virus between 2021 and 2023, according to a massive genetic analysis. Researchers found that viral transmission during that period was highest among school students between the ages of 15 and 18, university undergrads and nursing-home residents. However, staff at all three types of institution had about the same risk of contracting COVID-19 as did those in their surrounding communities. The study’s scale “is truly impressive”, says infectious-disease researcher Bill Hanage.

According to recent reports, A report by the US National Academies of Sciences, Engineering and Medicine (NASEM) suggests that science publishers take too long to retract or correct research papers, and standards for doing so are applied inconsistently across journals. NASEM recommends that the editorial review process be completed within 12 weeks for most cases and should rarely stretch beyond 6 months. The report was due to be published on 19 November, but was delayed after journalists at Science noted that it contained references with fabricated author names, which could suggest that artificial intelligence was used to draft or edit it.

Earlier this week we tried our hands at a game that tests our ability to decode ‘tortured phrases’ — ridiculous synonyms for common terms, which are intended to obscure plagiarism. For example, instead of ‘big data’, a study might use ‘colossal information’. The quiz inspired Briefing reader Chris Schneider to suggest her own tongue-in-cheek tortured phrase for our own dear ‘Nature Briefing’: “Essence of donning underwear.”.

In the spirit of silliness, we’d like to hear your best science-related tortured phrases — whether spotted in the wild or invented just for fun. Entertain us at briefing@nature.com.

Bees are the well-deserved superstars of the pollination world, and the reputations of birds, bats and even wasps are on the rise. Make room, now, for flies. Diptera — especially hoverflies (Syrphidae) — are undervalued pollinators. For example, on strawberry farms in England, hoverflies can make up more than half of the pollinating insects. Meanwhile, our reliance on managed honeybees can actually damage biodiversity and crop quality.

The Fresh Yorker | 16 min read (intermittent paywall).

An artificially intelligent human wants to make choices that matter in The right to do wrong.

In a recent development, for the first time, astrophysicists have directly observed a giant star — one that’s swelling in size toward the end of its life cycle — engulfing a nearby ‘companion’ star in its gas envelope. Now they wait to learn what comes next. The companion star could cause the giant star to shed its gas envelope, after which the two could settle into a tight orbit; or it could plunge into the giant star’s core to its doom. “To conclusively rule out either case, we need to continue observing the system,” says astrophysicist Viraj Karambelkar.

Space physicist Emma Bunce has been working on the European–Japanese BepiColombo mission for 20 years. After an eight-year journey battling the Sun's immense gravitational pull, if all goes well, it will finally enter Mercury’s orbit tomorrow. (The Guardian | 3 min read).
